clinical_significance: The single most clinically important bursa at the elbow: olecranon bursitis ('student's elbow'), whether traumatic (repetitive leaning/friction), septic, or crystal-induced (gout). It lies superficial to the triceps insertion, between skin and the olecranon, so a distended bursa presents as a superficial, mobile swelling directly over the olecranon rather than a deep joint effusion. Triceps trigger point TrP4 (deep and distal in the medial head, just above the olecranon) can clinically mimic olecranon bursitis, and the two should be distinguished on examination.
function: Reduces friction between the skin and the subcutaneous olecranon during elbow flexion/extension and direct pressure (e.g. leaning on the elbow).
source: Gray's Anatomy, 42nd ed. (Standring, ed.), Elsevier, 2021 -- bursae of the elbow; as cited in this atlas's uploaded elbow muscle reference document (elbow_muscles_reference_v2.html)

clinical_significance: Lies between the triceps tendon and the olecranon/posterior capsule, deep to the subcutaneous olecranon bursa. Inflammation presents as deep posterior elbow pain and can accompany insertional triceps tendinopathy, distinct from the superficial swelling of subcutaneous olecranon bursitis.
function: Reduces friction between the gliding triceps tendon and the underlying olecranon/posterior joint capsule during elbow extension.
source: Gray's Anatomy, 42nd ed. (Standring, ed.), Elsevier, 2021 -- bursae of the elbow; as cited in this atlas's uploaded elbow muscle reference document (elbow_muscles_reference_v2.html)

clinical_significance: Lies between the distal biceps tendon and the smooth anterior part of the radial tuberosity, wrapping the tendon; it is compressed between tendon and radial cortex during pronation. Distension presents as an antecubital mass with pain on pronation and can compress the posterior interosseous nerve (or the superficial radial nerve), producing PIN palsy-like or paraesthetic symptoms. May communicate with the interosseous cubital bursa but does not communicate with the elbow joint.
function: Reduces friction between the distal biceps tendon and the radial tuberosity as the tendon rotates with pronation/supination.
source: Skaf AY, Boutin RD, Dantas RW, et al. 'Bicipitoradial bursitis: MR imaging findings in eight patients and anatomic data from contrast opacification of bursae in cadavers.' Radiology 1999;212(1):111-116; Spinner RJ, Lins RE, Collins AJ, Spinner M. 'Posterior interosseous nerve compression due to an enlarged bicipital bursa confirmed by MRI.' J Hand Surg Br 1993;18(6):753-756 -- as cited in this atlas's uploaded elbow muscle reference document (elbow_muscles_reference_v2.html)

clinical_significance: Lies between the distal biceps tendon, supinator and the ulna. Presents the same way as bicipitoradial bursitis (antecubital mass, pain on pronation, possible posterior interosseous or superficial radial nerve compression); the two bursae may communicate with each other.
function: Reduces friction between the distal biceps tendon and adjacent supinator/ulna during pronosupination.
source: Gray's Anatomy, 42nd ed. (Standring, ed.), Elsevier, 2021 -- bursae of the elbow; as cited in this atlas's uploaded elbow muscle reference document (elbow_muscles_reference_v2.html)

clinical_significance: An inconstant bursa beneath the common extensor origin, over the radiohumeral joint. Proposed as a contributor to some cases of lateral epicondylar pain, though it is not a constant finding.
function: Where present, reduces friction between the common extensor origin (ECRB, extensor digitorum) and the underlying radiohumeral joint.
source: Gray's Anatomy, 42nd ed. (Standring, ed.), Elsevier, 2021 -- bursae of the elbow; as cited in this atlas's uploaded elbow muscle reference document (elbow_muscles_reference_v2.html)
